newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief condemns Rwanda killings; fifth man dies.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief condemns Rwanda killings; fifth man dies.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan condemned the ambush killing of human rights workers in Rwanda on Tuesday, saying he was "shocked and dismayed" at the slayings.

His spokesman Fred Eckhard said four human rights monitors -- a Briton, a Cambodian and two Rwandans -- were killed. A fifth, their Rwandan driver, died later in a hospital from stomach wounds, Eckhard said.
U.N. sources said the killings were particularly brutal.
"The secretary-general was shocked and dismayed by the news this morning that four human rights observers were killed and one was wounded," Eckhard said, adding that Annan condemned the deaths.

At the same time U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Jose Ayala Lasso "strongly condemned" the killings and said he ordered human rights officers in Cyangugu, Gisenji and Kibuye areas to evacuate to Kigali.
The order to retreat to Kigali affected some 15 of the 139 U.N. human rights officers working throughout the country to protect and promote human rights, U.N. sources said.
Eckhard identified the dead as a Cambodian serving as a U.N. volunteer, a Briton with the U.N. field operation in Rwanda and two local Rwandan employees.
All were travelling in a marked U.N. vehicle.
The Rwandan government made a helicopter available to U.N. security officials who went to the scene of the attack, Eckhard said.
The five were killed while visiting a commune of Karengera in Cyangugu prefecture, approximately 200 miles (350 km) southwest of Kigali on the Zairean border.
Ayala Lasso, travelling on Tuesday in the United States, issued his comments in a statement released in New York and Geneva where his commission is based.
"I strongly condemn this attack and offer my deepest sympathy to the families of those killed," he said.

Ayala Lasso, a former U.N. ambassador from Ecuador, who was named to the new post three years ago, said: "This is the first loss of life resulting from an attack in the Human Rights Field Operation in Rwanda."

"These deaths demonstrate once again the urgent need to work in order to ensure respect for human rights and to establish in Rwanda a climate of peaceful relations among all communities," Ayala-Lasso said.

Xavier Zuniga, a Mexican who heads the U.N. human rights field operation in Rwanda, as well as Omar Bakhet, resident coordinator of the U.N. Development Programme in Kigali, went to Cyangugu to begin the investigation, according to the statement. The UNDP chief acts as a security coordinator.

A U.N. report issued by his Geneva office last Friday said Hutu death squads in Rwanda were killing Tutsi survivors of genocide and witnesses who were forced to move out of isolated areas near army positions in search of security.
More than half a million minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates died in 1994's Hutu-led ethnic slaughter, after which Tutsis swept to power in Rwanda and the perpetrators fled to neighbouring countries.

In total the U.N. human rights office in Rwanda received reports of nearly 1,600 killings in 1996. It gave no breakdown for killings by the Tutsi-dominated army which is fighting an insurgency by rebels of the Hutu majority.
